Title: The Old Man and the Sea
Author: Ernest Hemingway
My Review:
In modern times, this book feels anti-algorithmic.

One fisherman. One boat. Blood, salt, fatigue.

Too far out in the sea for hours where nothing happens.

The nothingness is the medium with which Hemingway conveys everything. The struggle, the restraint, the wrestle with a challenge.

Almost like punching a bag for hours. There’s rhythm, no arc.

A book about maintaining form under pressure. 

Santiago, the fisherman, doesn’t “discover” himself in the sea. He doesn’t transform. He doesn’t resolve a psychological arc. He holds the line. That’s it.

Hemingway’s ethic is brutally conservative here: dignity is not self-expression or growth; dignity is not breaking.

The book is not inspiring nor magnetic, just coherent.

Title: Why The Poor Don’t Kill Us
Subtitle: The Psychology of Indians
Author: Manu Joseph
My Review:
I was introduced to Manu Joseph via a show he created that’s on Netflix, “Decoupled”.

It’s the kind of a show that made me want to learn more about who developed it instead of being a mere consumer of the plot. It’s when I noticed the work of Manu Joseph, who, in this book, splendidly conveys the nature of India in all its absurdities.

Decoupled felt refreshing, unique, well-written. It hilariously showcased the Indian class divide and it grappled with idea of how India treats money, class, religion.

Why The Poor Don’t Kill Us feels like an extension of sorts. At times, I read certain excerpts with the voice of R. Madhavan who plays the protagonist in the show Decoupled. It was hard to me for decouple the show with the book.

Now, the book asserts the psychology of Indians across different socio-economic backgrounds and talks about ideas like how the aesthetic ugliness of the country reassures the poor, our outlook towards money and how it makes sense for rich moneylenders to prefer an austere life, how material success is more powerful than mere activism to bring real change.

It is a darkly hilarious book that will make you laugh, and then leave you uncomfortable because you laughed. It confronts a reality that is deeply relevant to the Indian society in a bold, unapologetic	fashion that leaves you surprised because what you read in this book is what you live around, everyday, without noticing.

Title: The Stranger
Author: Albert Camus
My Review:
I haven’t read fiction this arresting in a long time. The opening line alone is so remarkable that I had to take a pause and gear up for what followed. The story of Meursault is that he fails to live with a narrative to please societal expectations.

Camus stages a thought experiment with the help of Meursault: What happens if a man refuses to lie emotionally in a world that requires it?

The book is about the punishment you get for not living up to social expectations regardless of how you feel.

Meursault is ruthless, but in an honest way that intends no harm for others and yet, he’s punished for being that way.

About the writing, Matthew Ward’s translation serves as a charming, magnetic outlook into the story of Meursault. It’s easy to step into his world, but impossible to judge his actions comfortably.

A lot more thoughts to be shared, a lot more conversations to be had about this book.

Timeless.

Hemingway’s ethic is brutally conservative here: dignity is not self-expression or growth; dignity is not breaking.

The book is not inspiring nor magnetic, just coherent.

Title: Why The Poor Don’t Kill Us
Subtitle: The Psychology of Indians
Author: Manu Joseph
My Review:
I was introduced to Manu Joseph via a show he created that’s on Netflix, “Decoupled”.

It’s the kind of a show that made me want to learn more about who developed it instead of being a mere consumer of the plot. It’s when I noticed the work of Manu Joseph, who, in this book, splendidly conveys the nature of India in all its absurdities.

Decoupled felt refreshing, unique, well-written. It hilariously showcased the Indian class divide and it grappled with idea of how India treats money, class, religion.

Why The Poor Don’t Kill Us feels like an extension of sorts. At times, I read certain excerpts with the voice of R. Madhavan who plays the protagonist in the show Decoupled. It was hard to me for decouple the show with the book.

Now, the book asserts the psychology of Indians across different socio-economic backgrounds and talks about ideas like how the aesthetic ugliness of the country reassures the poor, our outlook towards money and how it makes sense for rich moneylenders to prefer an austere life, how material success is more powerful than mere activism to bring real change.

It is a darkly hilarious book that will make you laugh, and then leave you uncomfortable because you laughed. It confronts a reality that is deeply relevant to the Indian society in a bold, unapologetic	fashion that leaves you surprised because what you read in this book is what you live around, everyday, without noticing.

Title: The Stranger
Author: Albert Camus
My Review:
I haven’t read fiction this arresting in a long time. The opening line alone is so remarkable that I had to take a pause and gear up for what followed. The story of Meursault is that he fails to live with a narrative to please societal expectations.

Camus stages a thought experiment with the help of Meursault: What happens if a man refuses to lie emotionally in a world that requires it?

The book is about the punishment you get for not living up to social expectations regardless of how you feel.

Meursault is ruthless, but in an honest way that intends no harm for others and yet, he’s punished for being that way.

About the writing, Matthew Ward’s translation serves as a charming, magnetic outlook into the story of Meursault. It’s easy to step into his world, but impossible to judge his actions comfortably.

A lot more thoughts to be shared, a lot more conversations to be had about this book.

Timeless.
